method: MIXED. L1 and L2 are AMH's Local anaesthesia topic and Local anaesthetics class page including its Comparison of some local anaesthetics table, paraphrased, no passage stored: the maximum doses, the vasoconstrictor rules and the toxicity picture. S1 is the OPEN RACGP AJGP article 'Skin procedures in general practice' (August 2024), quoted verbatim, for the setting in which an Australian GP most often gives a local anaesthetic. S2 is an OPEN RACGP AJGP PILOT STUDY from the same issue relating lignocaine dose and volume to wound complications -- quoted verbatim TOGETHER WITH THE AUTHORS' OWN STATEMENT THAT ITS SHORTCOMINGS LIMIT ATTRIBUTION OF FINDINGS TO CLINICAL PRACTICE, and with a limitation visible in its own data. NO CLAIM FROM S2 IS USED TO SET A DOSE OR A LIMIT; AMH's maxima are the only maxima here.

claims.claim: The most common complications of skin excision are WOUND DEHISCENCE AND/OR INFECTION, and well-described risk factors include PATIENT AGE OVER 80 YEARS AND EXCISIONS ON THE LIMBS; in this study, lesions on the LIMBS or MALIGNANT ON HISTOLOGY had a significant positive relationship with the complication rate
claims.source_text: The most common complications are wound dehiscence and/or infection. … Significant risk factors for such complications are well described in the literature and include patient age >80 years and excisions on the limbs. … However, lesions either located on the limbs or malignant upon histology were found to have a significant positive relationship with the complication rate.

claims.source_text: This represents a unique contribution to the literature because previous research into complications after skin cancer excision has not considered local anaesthetic as a contributor to wound healing. … research examining complications after skin cancer excisions does not consider lignocaine as a risk factor, whereas wound healing research is inconclusive with regard to the effects of lignocaine
